episode_title: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate

stories.topic: Larry White and the World of Competing Currencies
stories.summary: Amit opens by describing his recent Seen and the Unseen conversation with Larry White, author of The Clash of Economic Ideas and a leading expert on free banking. White studied periods in different countries where there was no single official currency from a central bank. Instead, several banks issued their own competing currencies. The instinctive reaction is that this would be chaos: who do you trust, and how would the currencies work together? White's papers and books show the system worked very well. Some early crypto pioneers, including people thought to be possible Satoshi Nakamotos, cited his papers.
stories.insight: Even the state's monopoly on money, which feels like a law of nature, was a historical choice. That is Amit's Dylan point: don't assume that how things are is the only way they can be.
stories.quote: as his papers and his books point out, it worked marvelously well

stories.topic: The Daily Benzene Ship Across the Gulf of Gujarat
stories.summary: Ajay recalls something from his time on a company board. Every day, Reliance sent one ship of benzene from its refinery at Jamnagar to an Indian buyer on the other side of the Gulf of Gujarat. Seller and buyer were both Indian and the trip was short. Even so, the contract price was the Korean price of benzene multiplied by the exchange rate, so it changed every day.
stories.insight: This is import parity pricing at work. For any globally traded commodity, the exchange rate reaches into transactions that never leave India, which is why the rupee matters far beyond importers and exporters.
stories.quote: And the price was the Korean price of benzene multiplied by the exchange rate.

stories.topic: The Oil That Hadn't Left the Middle East Yet
stories.summary: When Ajay was very young, the Middle Eastern producers, angry at losing the Yom Kippur war, quadrupled crude oil from $2 to $8. He remembers laughing out loud at people asking why prices in India and California had risen immediately, when the ship carrying the expensive oil had not even left the Middle East.
stories.insight: Prices move at the speed of information, not the speed of ships. Oil or steel already in storage carries no label showing what was paid for it, so the moment the world price changes, every unit everywhere is repriced.
stories.quote: The crude oil doesn't carry a price labeled on top of it. So the moment a price changes, prices everywhere change.

stories.topic: George Soros Bets Against the Bank of England
stories.summary: Ajay uses Britain as an example of a country that is now out of the currency business. The Bank of England once tried to distort the currency market. George Soros saw that it could not hold that position and placed a huge bet that the Bank would fail. He is reputed to have made a billion in one day. Amit calls it one man betting against the might of the British state, and winning.
stories.insight: A central bank defending an artificial exchange rate is fighting the market, and the market can win. Lessons like this are partly why advanced economies stopped trying to manage their currencies.
stories.quote: the great man George Soros understood that correctly and had the courage of his convictions to put a large bet on that market

stories.topic: The 1966 Devaluation That Paid Off Later
stories.summary: In the controlled era, every exchange rate change was a policy decision. The famous one was Indira Gandhi's 1966 depreciation. Ajay says most people misjudge it because they look only at 1967 to 1969. Large exchange rate moves affect imports and exports with a time lag. By the early-seventies oil shock, export and import shifts were under way, and that helped India handle the shock relatively well.
stories.insight: Judge macroeconomic moves over the right time horizon. A policy that looks like it did little in the first couple of years may be what saves you later.
stories.quote: It sandbagged the economy in time for the oil shock of the early seventies.

stories.topic: Ashok Desai and Each Generation's Young Turk Idea
stories.summary: Ashok Desai was Manmohan Singh's chief economic advisor in 1991 and drafted the July 1991 budget speech. He once told Ajay that his own generation's big idea was openness to international trade, and they mocked their predecessors for believing in trade barriers. He said Ajay's generation's idea was exchange rate flexibility and an open capital account. He added that when he talked about controls on the exchange rate, he could see Ajay's generation looking at him and wondering what was wrong with him.
stories.insight: Reform is a relay. Each generation's radical idea becomes the next generation's common sense, and Ajay places India somewhere in the middle of that long journey.
stories.quote: in your generation, the Young Turk idea is exchange rate flexibility and openness on the capital account.

stories.topic: When India Tasted a Floating Rupee
stories.summary: Under RBI Governor Subbarao, roughly from 2007 to 2012-13, India had a lot of exchange rate flexibility. For long stretches the RBI did no trading on the currency market at all, even though many restrictions on market participants remained. When Raghuram Rajan became governor that period ended, and India went back to a heavily managed exchange rate.
stories.insight: India's choice is not between theory and the untested. It has already run a floating rupee for several years and then chose to retreat.
stories.quote: So we have tasted exchange rate flexibility, but unfortunately we just went back to the bad ideas and this is where we've been stuck ever since.

stories.topic: 'Desh Badalna Hai': The Origin of the Show
stories.summary: Months earlier, Amit found Ajay by the seaside and asked about his plan. Ajay said 'Desh badalna hai' (the country must change), with full stops and an exclamation mark in his voice. Amit told him the country won't change, and Ajay repeated himself. After some back and forth, Amit's answer was: don't worry, let's do YouTube. That, he says, is how Everything is Everything began.
stories.insight: Changing a country's ideas can begin with patient public explanation that reaches the next generation, rather than with policy levers.
stories.quote: So I said don't worry, YouTube karte hain. So that's story number four, the origin of the show. We can shape future generations who can hopefully badal the desh.

core_ideas.concept: The Exchange Rate Is the Most Important Price
core_ideas.explanation: The rupee-dollar rate touches importers and exporters, every domestic deal in globally traded goods, and the huge financial flows in and out of India. No other single price reaches so far into the economy.
core_ideas.quote: in the priceless words of Josh Felman, the exchange rate is the most important price of all.

core_ideas.explanation: The level of the exchange rate is just a unit. Japan trades at around 130 yen to the dollar and is one of the world's most successful countries. If India swapped every old rupee for ten new ones, the rate would jump from 80 to 800 and nothing real would change. Nationalist talk about rupee levels is innumeracy.
core_ideas.quote: It's as silly as counting my height in millimeters versus my height in inches and getting excited.

core_ideas.explanation: A depreciation from 80 to 90 makes a Rs 600 Tiruppur shirt cheaper for foreigners, so exporters gain. An appreciation from 80 to 70 makes a $100 imported phone and a trip to Greece cheaper, so consumers gain. There is no single 'good' direction; different people win and lose, as with any price.
core_ideas.quote: All prices cut both ways, and this is the first level at which we have to think.

core_ideas.explanation: Steel has one global market and one price, set on the London Metal Exchange. The Indian price is the LME price times the exchange rate. Tata Steel uses Indian ore, coal, power and labour, so when the rupee depreciates its costs stay the same while its rupee revenue rises, and the extra goes straight to operating profit. An appreciation does the reverse.
core_ideas.quote: For everybody in the world, the local price of steel is the LME price of steel multiplied by an exchange rate.

core_ideas.concept: Goods Arbitrage Holds the World Together
core_ideas.explanation: No planner or law sets a single world price. Traders watch steel prices in Singapore, Dubai, Visakhapatnam and Bombay, and ship goods whenever a gap opens, which closes the gap. Most people never check prices this way; a few profit-seeking arbitrageurs keep the world on one price for everyone, and Ajay notes there is an 'I, Pencil' story here.
core_ideas.quote: The chains of arbitrage hold prices together.

core_ideas.explanation: Many economists who don't know finance think the exchange rate is mainly about trade. That stopped being true decades ago. Capital flows such as FDI and portfolio investment now dominate the currency market, and trade is the smaller partner.
core_ideas.quote: Trade is a step sister compared to the size of finance.

core_ideas.concept: From Gold to Fiat: The Exchange Rate Became a Market Price
core_ideas.explanation: Money was first gold, then paper backed by gold. Later the US fixed $35 to an ounce of gold and other currencies were pegged to the dollar, an arrangement Keynes backed after the currency chaos of the Depression. Ajay thinks that design was unwise. It ended when Nixon took the US off gold and Bretton Woods collapsed. Currencies are now money by state decree, with no common anchor, so exchange rates are set by supply and demand. Milton Friedman was the first to see that governments don't need to be in this business.
core_ideas.quote: there is nothing in here other than the spirit of the Indian state. It is the Indian state that makes it so.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay sorts currency regimes into three types. In the first, like North Korea, the state is the counterparty to every currency transaction. In the second, like India, private transactions are allowed but tightly controlled and channelled through banks that earn a protected spread, while the central bank trades heavily to manage the rate. In the third, the advanced economies, the state stays out: Ajay believes the US Fed hasn't traded currencies since about 1994, and Japan and, recently, Switzerland are the exceptions. Knowing a country's regime explains a lot about the country.
core_ideas.quote: to understand a country you must understand its exchange rate system and the exchange rate regime.

core_ideas.concept: Floating Exchange Rates Are a Shock Absorber
core_ideas.explanation: In bad times such as floods, demonetisation or a breakdown of law and order, exports suffer and foreign investors pull money out, so the rupee depreciates. That makes exports more competitive, raises profits for import-parity producers, and makes imports dearer so demand shifts to Indian goods. In booms, the rupee appreciates and cools things down. The price system delivers stability with no official needed.
core_ideas.quote: That floating exchange rates stabilize the economy. They are a shock absorber.

core_ideas.concept: The Closet Bureaucrat and the Elite's Love of Stability
core_ideas.explanation: Indian elites accept fluctuating prices for steel, cement and nickel but want the rupee to stand still. The general rule still applies: prices are information wrapped in an incentive, and their movement is how the economy reallocates resources. Ajay argues policymakers fix the rupee to win the elite's applause, so the real audience to persuade is the elite.
core_ideas.quote: I think there's a closet bureaucrat inside each of us who just wants a simple unchanging life.

core_ideas.concept: Currency Controls Are Theft That Turns Citizens Into Criminals
core_ideas.explanation: Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off. Controls that block or slow such exchanges destroy value that we never get to see. They also force ordinary people to break the law just to do things with their own money.
core_ideas.quote: this is not merely coercion. It is also theft.

core_ideas.concept: FERA, FEMA and the Inverted Default
core_ideas.explanation: FERA, passed in the 1970s, made foreign exchange dealings a crime; being caught with dollar bills could get you into trouble. Ajay says economic offences need only civil fines, such as three times the ill-gotten gain. FEMA replaced FERA in 1999, but criminal clauses returned in 2015. FEMA starts by banning all cross-border activity and then lists what is permitted. It is enforced by an Enforcement Directorate whose law gives it raid powers without proper rule of law. The result is a maze of circulars that keeps lawyers and accountants busy.
core_ideas.quote: Freedom should be the norm. And maybe you have some exceptions, and we can debate what the exceptions should be.

core_ideas.concept: The Blind Spot of the 1991 Reformers
core_ideas.explanation: The 1991 generation understood economics but not law, public administration or public choice theory. They gave bodies like the RBI wide arbitrary powers, assuming good people like themselves would always run them. Amit compares this to Nehru's generation writing a constitution that protects the state from the people rather than the other way round.
core_ideas.quote: Many times they thought that people like me will be running these organizations, now, and how can it go so bad because I'm a good guy.

core_ideas.concept: Controls Only Bind the Little Guy
core_ideas.explanation: Restrictions always create a black market. The legal route needs expensive lawyers, so only the top 0.1% can buy a Nasdaq ETF or a flat in London. Firms move money through misinvoicing: billing a 100 export at 110 brings 10 into India on the quiet. These hidden flows dwarf the formal ones.
core_ideas.quote: If you are anybody other than the top 0.1%, it's a closed capital account.

core_ideas.concept: Internationalisation Is the Engine of Growth
core_ideas.explanation: Trade, FDI and foreign capital arrive as a package of knowledge that raises a country's productivity and capabilities. Every friction placed on cross-border engagement therefore slows growth itself.
core_ideas.quote: So internationalization is the package through which you obtain economic growth.

core_ideas.concept: Cross the River by Feeling the Stones
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay is conservative about reform method. Central planning is dismantled one regulation at a time, by persuading people that each rule makes no sense. That needs full-time teams who study data, talk to practitioners and write publicly. India once had such a community for currency reform but no longer does, so nothing is moving.
core_ideas.quote: You should cross a river by feeling the stones.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Targeting Is the Poured Foundation
core_ideas.explanation: One piece is in good shape. The RBI is now accountable for an inflation target, not for delivering a particular exchange rate or exchange rate stability. That makes the right reform possible: a clean law where all transactions are legal with a few exceptions, real current account convertibility, and few capital account controls.
core_ideas.quote: RBI is accountable for delivering an inflation target, and this is correct.

core_ideas.concept: Amit's Arc of India's Economic Journey
core_ideas.explanation: Nehru built democratic institutions but distrusted markets, and his mistakes were reversible. Indira's economic policies, including FERA, bank nationalisation, labour laws and a 97% peak income tax rate, were in Amit's view crimes on humanity. Then came the quiet reformers, 1991, and twenty golden years with consensus across parties that lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Since roughly 2011-12, Amit says, India has gone backwards.
core_ideas.quote: Our current Prime Minister has the top down thinking of Nehru and the authoritarian impulses of Indira and an ignorance of economics of both of them, frankly.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay pitches his redenomination thought experiment as 'better than demonetization', and Amit shoots back: 'That was the worst possible thing. Everything is better.'

After Ajay compares the rupee-level obsession to measuring height in millimetres instead of inches, Amit says: 'People who live in a country called millimeter must be feeling damn jealous of people who live in a country called Inch.'

Ajay pictures the business elite of Bengal, 'the blood relatives of Rabindranath Tagore', engaged in 'the highly intellectual activity' of watching steel prices in Singapore and Dubai. Later, when Ajay imagines a 'skeptical Bengali' who trusts markets everywhere except exchange rates, Amit replies: 'I'm not that kind of Bengali. In everything markets are good.'
Ajay on economists: 'Trade is some minor thing that real people do. The really big thing in the world is called finance.'
Amit, defending wonkish economics episodes: 'No man, this shit has humanitarian consequences.'
Since the monetary economics episode is coming next, Amit tells viewers to 'watch it at 0.25X so it'll last and last and last till we get there.'

Ajay keeps invoking 'every dentist and grandmother in Connecticut or Kyoto' rushing into or out of Indian assets. Amit: 'If you happen to be a grandmother and a dentist at the same time and live dual lives in Connecticut and Kyoto, come to our arms.'

Ajay calls FEMA 'an employment guarantee program for lawyers and accountants', and mocks its absurd detail: 'If you are a foreign investor who is a dentist investing in nanotechnology, then we will permit you to do ECB and you have to fill form number 74, EE1.'

Amit, who says his are 'the best show notes in the world... Never a mistake', reveals the one error ever made in them. Ajay sent his favourite papers at the last minute and listed the co-author of his misinvoicing paper as Abhijit Banerjee instead of Abhijit Sen Gupta. Amit pasted it in at 2:30 AM. In this episode Ajay pointedly says: 'Abhijit Sengupta. Not Abhijit Banerjee.'

Amit reveals that Ajay has a cat named FEMA. Ajay's cover story is that the cat fell from a third-floor house as a kitten and broke its femur. Amit: 'Oh, so it's not FEMA, it's femur. Is that what you're claiming?' The verdict: Ajay is a one-track mind, and all he thinks about is exchange rates.

Amit: 'Ajay has watched twenty films in the last twenty years. Eleven of them are the Matrix.' Amit, Vaishnav and Nomsita got him to agree to one film a month from each of them. He thought they would vote and agree on one, and months later he still hasn't watched either of Amit's picks. His defence: 'It's a big life change, okay? I have to implement it.'
Bob Dylan's line 'he not busy being born is busy dying', which Amit uses to open the episode as a warning against taking how things are for granted. He uses it again in the Life Lessons pitch.

Subramanian Swamy, then advising the party in opposition, said the rupee should be at 1 to the dollar. Amit calls it 'complete madness'. Today that party is in power and gets mocked for the rupee sliding past 80.
Nehru once told JRD Tata: 'Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.' Amit cites it as the spirit of top-down Nehruvian economics.

Keynes backing a fixed, gold-linked post-war currency order, Nixon taking the US off gold, and the 'collapse of Bretton Woods' that started the era of fiat money and floating rates. Ajay says governments are still 'going through their stages of grief' about it.
